1.summary: The risen Jesus teaches for forty days, promises the Holy Spirit, and ascends; the disciples pray together in Jerusalem and choose Matthias to replace Judas.
1.lookfor: Notice the disciples' question about the kingdom and how Jesus redirects it, and the plan for the whole book in verse 8.

names.name: Theophilus
names.gloss: The person Luke wrote his Gospel and Acts for.

names.name: Olivet
names.gloss: The Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem.

names.name: Matthias
names.gloss: A follower of Jesus from the beginning, chosen by lot to replace Judas.

names.name: Barsabbas
names.gloss: Joseph called Barsabbas, also named Justus, the other candidate.

insights.title: All that Jesus began
insights.body: Luke calls his Gospel the account of all that Jesus began to do and teach (1:1). Acts is the continuation: what the risen Jesus keeps doing through his Spirit and his people.

insights.title: Restore the kingdom to Israel?
insights.body: The disciples ask if now is the time to restore the kingdom to Israel (1:6). Jesus doesn't deny the hope but changes the focus: not the timing, but power to be witnesses everywhere.

insights.title: The book in one verse
insights.body: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, the ends of the earth (1:8) is the outline of Acts: chapters 1–7 in Jerusalem, 8–12 in Judea and Samaria, 13–28 to Rome. Isaiah's servant was to be a light to the ends of the earth.

insights.title: Witnesses
insights.body: The Greek word for witness, martys (1:8), meant someone who testifies to what they've seen. Because so many witnesses died for their testimony, the word later came to mean martyr.

insights.title: Taken up in a cloud
insights.body: Jesus is taken up and a cloud hides him (1:9), recalling Daniel's Son of Man coming with the clouds to the Ancient of Days. The angels promise he will return the same way (1:11).

insights.title: Casting lots
insights.body: The apostles pray and cast lots between two candidates (1:26), an old way of leaving the decision to God. It is the last time lots are used to discern God's will in the Bible; after Pentecost the Spirit guides.

insights.title: Waiting together
insights.body: Before the Spirit comes, about 120 believers wait and pray together (1:14-15). What are you trying to do in your own strength that needs to start with waiting and prayer?

2.summary: At Pentecost the Holy Spirit comes with wind and fire, the believers speak in many languages, Peter preaches that Jesus is Lord and Christ, three thousand are baptized and the church shares life together.
2.lookfor: Notice how many nations are listed, what the crowd hears, and what the new believers devote themselves to.

names.name: Parthians
names.gloss: People from the Parthian empire east of Rome, beyond the Euphrates.

names.name: Medes
names.gloss: People from Media, in modern Iran.

names.name: Elamites
names.gloss: People from Elam, east of Babylon.

names.name: Mesopotamia
names.gloss: The land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

names.name: Cappadocia
names.gloss: A region in central Asia Minor (modern Turkey).

names.name: Joel
names.gloss: An Old Testament prophet who foretold the Spirit poured on all people.

insights.title: The day of Pentecost
insights.body: Pentecost, the Feast of Weeks, came fifty days after Passover (2:1) and celebrated the wheat harvest. Later Jewish tradition also linked it to the giving of the law at Sinai, which came with fire and sound.

insights.title: Babel undone
insights.body: At Babel God confused languages and scattered the nations; at Pentecost people from every nation hear God's works in their own languages (2:6-11). Many readers see Pentecost reversing Babel, uniting without erasing differences.

insights.title: Joel's promise
insights.body: Peter explains with Joel's prophecy: in the last days God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh, sons and daughters, old and young, servants (2:17-18). The Spirit is no longer for a few prophets but for all God's people.

insights.title: David's tomb
insights.body: Peter quotes Psalm 16, about God not letting his Holy One see decay, and points out that David's tomb is still there (2:29). David spoke of the Messiah's resurrection, not his own.

insights.title: Lord and Christ
insights.body: Peter's climax: God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ (2:36). The crowd is cut to the heart and asks what to do.

insights.title: Four marks of the church
insights.body: The new believers devote themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer (2:42). They share possessions so no one is in need, fulfilling the law's hope that there be no poor among them.

insights.title: What shall we do?
insights.body: The crowd asks, "What shall we do?" and Peter answers: repent and be baptized (2:37-38). What would repentance mean for you this week, in concrete terms?

3.summary: Peter and John heal a man lame from birth at the temple gate, and Peter tells the amazed crowd that the healing came through faith in Jesus, whom they killed and God raised.
3.lookfor: Notice what the lame man asks for and what he gets instead, and the titles Peter gives Jesus.

names.name: Beautiful
names.gloss: A temple gate, probably the Nicanor Gate of bronze on the east side.

names.name: Solomon
names.gloss: Israel's king; a colonnade on the temple's east side bore his name.

names.name: Samuel
names.gloss: The prophet who anointed David, first of the prophets after Moses.

insights.title: The hour of prayer
insights.body: Peter and John go up at the ninth hour, about three in the afternoon (3:1), the time of the evening sacrifice and prayer. The first believers still worshiped in the temple.

insights.title: No silver or gold
insights.body: The man asks for money; Peter says, "I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you" (3:6), and heals him in Jesus' name. He receives far more than he asked.

insights.title: Leaping like a deer
insights.body: The man walks, leaps and praises God in the temple (3:8). Isaiah promised that in the age of God's rescue the lame would leap like a deer.

insights.title: The Author of life
insights.body: Peter says they killed the Prince or Author of life (3:15); the Greek archēgos means founder, leader or pioneer. The irony is sharp: they put to death the source of life, and God raised him.

insights.title: In ignorance
insights.body: Peter says the people and their rulers acted in ignorance (3:17), echoing Jesus' prayer from the cross. Their guilt is real, but so is the open door: repent, so your sins may be blotted out.

insights.title: The prophet like Moses
insights.body: Peter cites Moses' promise of a prophet like him whom Israel must hear (3:22) and God's promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed through his seed (3:25).

insights.title: Look at us
insights.body: Peter says, "Look at us" (3:4), then quickly turns attention to Jesus (3:12). How do you point people beyond yourself to him?

4.summary: Peter and John are arrested and boldly tell the council there is salvation in no other name; released, the believers pray for boldness, the place shakes, and they share everything in common.
4.lookfor: Notice what amazes the council about Peter and John, and what the believers pray for after the threat (not safety).

names.name: Sadducees
names.gloss: The priestly party that denied the resurrection.

names.name: Annas
names.gloss: A former high priest who remained powerful.

names.name: Caiaphas
names.gloss: The serving high priest, who had handed Jesus to Pilate.

names.name: Alexander
names.gloss: A member of the high-priestly family.

names.name: Barnabas
names.gloss: Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, renamed Son of Encouragement.

names.name: Cyprus
names.gloss: A large island in the eastern Mediterranean.

insights.title: Why the Sadducees were upset
insights.body: The Sadducees were annoyed that the apostles proclaimed resurrection in Jesus (4:2). They denied any resurrection, and a risen Jesus was living proof against them.

insights.title: No other name
insights.body: Peter tells the council that salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (4:12). The name of Jesus runs through these chapters as the power behind every healing.

insights.title: Unschooled men
insights.body: The council sees that Peter and John are uneducated, ordinary men and is amazed at their boldness; they recognize that they had been with Jesus (4:13). "Uneducated" meant without formal training in the law, not illiterate.

insights.title: Why do the nations rage?
insights.body: The believers pray Psalm 2, about rulers gathering against the Lord's anointed, and name Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel as its fulfillment (4:25-27).

insights.title: Boldness
insights.body: The believers pray not for protection but for boldness (4:29), the Greek parrēsia, free and fearless speech. The place shakes, and they speak the word with boldness (4:31).

insights.title: Son of Encouragement
insights.body: Barnabas sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet (4:36-37). He will reappear as the encourager who vouches for Saul and travels with him.

insights.title: Praying for boldness
insights.body: Threatened, they pray for courage, not comfort (4:29). What would you pray for if you faced pressure for your faith?

5.summary: Ananias and Sapphira die after lying about their gift; the apostles heal many, are jailed and freed by an angel, and the respected teacher Gamaliel persuades the council to let them go.
5.lookfor: Notice what Ananias and Sapphira's sin actually was, and Gamaliel's argument about movements from God.

names.name: Ananias
names.gloss: A man who lied about the price of his land.

names.name: Sapphira
names.gloss: Ananias's wife, who shared in the lie.

names.name: Gamaliel
names.gloss: A leading Pharisee and teacher of the law, Paul's teacher.

names.name: Theudas
names.gloss: A man who claimed to be somebody and led a failed movement.

insights.title: The lie, not the amount
insights.body: Peter tells Ananias the land was his and the money his to use (5:4). The sin was not keeping some back but pretending to give everything, lying to the Holy Spirit (5:3).

insights.title: Achan and the new beginning
insights.body: The judgment on Ananias and Sapphira recalls Achan, who secretly kept devoted goods as Israel entered the land. At founding moments, God's holiness is shown with special severity.

insights.title: Peter's shadow
insights.body: People lay the sick in the streets so that even Peter's shadow might fall on them (5:15). The healing power that worked through Jesus' cloak now works through his apostles.

insights.title: Obey God rather than men
insights.body: Ordered to stop teaching, Peter says, "We must obey God rather than men" (5:29). The line became a classic statement of conscience before human authority.

insights.title: Gamaliel's caution
insights.body: Gamaliel recalls Theudas and Judas of Galilee, whose movements collapsed after they died (5:36-37). Leave these men alone: if this is from people it will fail; if from God, you can't stop it. The historian Josephus also mentions Judas the Galilean.

insights.title: Rejoicing in dishonor
insights.body: Flogged, the apostles leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the Name (5:41), as Jesus had said: blessed are you when people insult you.

insights.title: Appearances
insights.body: Ananias wanted credit for generosity he didn't have. Where are you tempted to look more devoted than you are?

6.summary: When Greek-speaking widows are overlooked, the church chooses seven men to serve; the word spreads, and Stephen, full of grace and power, is falsely accused before the council.
6.lookfor: Notice how the apostles handle the complaint, and the names of the seven (all Greek).

names.name: Hellenists
names.gloss: Greek-speaking Jews, often from outside Judea.

names.name: Stephen
names.gloss: One of the seven, the first Christian martyr.

names.name: Prochorus
names.gloss: One of the seven chosen to serve.

names.name: Nicanor
names.gloss: One of the seven.

names.name: Timon
names.gloss: One of the seven.

names.name: Parmenas
names.gloss: One of the seven.

names.name: Nicolaus
names.gloss: One of the seven, a convert to Judaism from Antioch.

names.name: Libertines
names.gloss: A synagogue of freedmen, Jews who were former slaves or their descendants.

insights.title: Two kinds of Jews
insights.body: The complaint comes from Hellenists, Greek-speaking Jews, against Hebrews, Aramaic-speaking Jews (6:1). Widows without family depended on the church's daily food distribution.

insights.title: Seven Greek names
insights.body: All seven chosen have Greek names (6:5). The church gives responsibility to people from the group that was overlooked, which helps end the complaint.

insights.title: Prayer and the word
insights.body: The apostles say they must devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word (6:4), not because serving tables is beneath them, but because each task needs full attention. The word for serving is the root of deacon.

insights.title: Priests believed
insights.body: A great number of priests become obedient to the faith (6:7). Many priests were poor and served in rotation, unlike the ruling high-priestly families.

insights.title: Like Jesus' trial
insights.body: Stephen's accusers bring false witnesses saying he spoke against the temple and the law (6:13-14), the same charges brought against Jesus. Stephen follows his Lord's path.

insights.title: The face of an angel
insights.body: The council sees Stephen's face like the face of an angel (6:15). Moses' face shone after meeting God; Stephen is about to defend his faith using Moses' own story.

insights.title: Overlooked people
insights.body: The church noticed a group being overlooked and acted. Who in your church or circle is being overlooked?

7.summary: Stephen retells Israel's story to show that God was never confined to one land or building and that Israel always resisted its deliverers; enraged, the council stones him as he prays for them.
7.lookfor: Watch how often Stephen points out that God met people outside the land, and what Stephen sees as he dies.

names.name: Mesopotamia
names.gloss: The land between the rivers, where Abraham first lived.

names.name: Haran
names.gloss: A city in northern Mesopotamia where Abraham stayed.

names.name: Shechem
names.gloss: A town in Samaria where Jacob's family was buried.

names.name: Midian
names.gloss: A desert region where Moses fled and lived forty years.

names.name: Sinai
names.gloss: The mountain where God gave the law.

names.name: Saul
names.gloss: A young Pharisee, later Paul, who approved of Stephen's death.

skim.advice: Verses 2 to 47 retell Israel's story from Abraham to Solomon; skim the history and notice the pattern of rejected deliverers, then read verses 48 to 60 closely.

insights.title: God outside the land
insights.body: Stephen shows God appearing to Abraham in Mesopotamia, with Joseph in Egypt and to Moses in Midian (7:2, 7:9, 7:30). God was never limited to the land or the temple, which answers the charge that he spoke against the holy place.

insights.title: Rejected deliverers
insights.body: Joseph's brothers sold him, and Israel rejected Moses: who made you a ruler? (7:35). The pattern of rejecting God's chosen deliverer reaches its climax with Jesus.

insights.title: Not in houses made with hands
insights.body: Stephen quotes Isaiah: heaven is my throne and earth my footstool; what house will you build me? (7:49). Solomon himself prayed that heaven could not contain God.

insights.title: Stiff-necked
insights.body: Stephen calls the council stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart (7:51), using God's own words about Israel at the golden calf. Uncircumcised in heart means outwardly in the covenant but inwardly resistant.

insights.title: The Son of Man standing
insights.body: Stephen sees the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand (7:56). Elsewhere Jesus is seated there; many readers think he stands to receive or vindicate his witness.

insights.title: He died like his Lord
insights.body: Stephen prays, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit, and, Lord, don't hold this sin against them (7:59-60), echoing Jesus' words from the cross.

insights.title: Saul was watching
insights.body: The witnesses lay their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul (7:58). What do you make of the fact that Stephen's death set the stage for Paul's story?

8.summary: Persecution scatters the believers; Philip preaches in Samaria, where Simon the sorcerer tries to buy the Spirit's power, and then explains Isaiah to an Ethiopian official, who is baptized on the road.
8.lookfor: Notice how persecution spreads the message instead of stopping it, and who Philip reaches: Samaritans and a foreign eunuch.

names.name: Philip
names.gloss: One of the seven, later called the evangelist; not the apostle Philip.

names.name: Samaria
names.gloss: The region between Judea and Galilee, home of the Samaritans.

names.name: Simon
names.gloss: A sorcerer in Samaria who tried to buy the power to give the Spirit.

names.name: Candace
names.gloss: A title of the queens of Ethiopia (ancient Nubia, south of Egypt).

names.name: Gaza
names.gloss: An old Philistine city on the road from Jerusalem to Egypt.

names.name: Azotus
names.gloss: The Greek name of Ashdod, on the coast.

insights.title: Scattered seed
insights.body: After Stephen's death, everyone except the apostles is scattered through Judea and Samaria (8:1), exactly the next step of 1:8. Those scattered go about preaching the word (8:4).

insights.title: Samaritans
insights.body: Jews and Samaritans had been divided for centuries over worship and ancestry. That Samaria receives the word, and that Peter and John come to pray for them, marks a deep breach being healed.

insights.title: Simony
insights.body: Simon offers money for the power to give the Spirit, and Peter rebukes him: may your silver perish with you (8:20). Buying church offices came to be called simony after him.

insights.title: Why the Spirit waited
insights.body: The Samaritans believe and are baptized, but receive the Spirit only when Peter and John arrive (8:15-17). Many readers see this as tying the Samaritan believers to the Jerusalem church, so there would be one church, not two rival ones.

insights.title: The eunuch and Isaiah
insights.body: The Ethiopian reads Isaiah 53, the servant led like a sheep to slaughter (8:32), and Philip begins there to tell him about Jesus. Isaiah also promised that faithful eunuchs and foreigners would have a place in God's house.

insights.title: What prevents me?
insights.body: Seeing water, the eunuch asks what keeps him from being baptized (8:36). A man barred from the temple's inner courts finds nothing barring him from Christ.

insights.title: Do you understand what you read?
insights.body: Philip asks, and the eunuch answers that he needs someone to guide him (8:30-31). Who helps you understand Scripture, and whom could you help?

9.summary: On the road to Damascus, Saul the persecutor meets the risen Jesus and is blinded; Ananias heals and baptizes him, he preaches Jesus and escapes plots; Peter heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha.
9.lookfor: Notice who Jesus says Saul is persecuting, and Ananias's courage in going to him.

names.name: Damascus
names.gloss: A major city in Syria, northeast of Galilee.

names.name: Ananias
names.gloss: A believer in Damascus sent to heal Saul; not the man of chapter 5.

names.name: Tarsus
names.gloss: Saul's home city in Cilicia, in southeast Asia Minor.

names.name: Lydda
names.gloss: A town on the plain inland from Joppa.

names.name: Aeneas
names.gloss: A man paralyzed for eight years, healed by Peter.

names.name: Joppa
names.gloss: A port on the coast, modern Jaffa.

names.name: Tabitha
names.gloss: A disciple known for good works, also called Dorcas; both names mean gazelle.

insights.title: The Way
insights.body: Saul hunts anyone belonging to the Way (9:2), one of the earliest names for the Jesus movement. Jesus had called himself the way.

insights.title: Why do you persecute me?
insights.body: Jesus asks Saul why he persecutes me (9:4), not my followers. What is done to Jesus' people is done to him, an idea Paul later develops in the church as Christ's body.

insights.title: A chosen vessel
insights.body: Ananias is afraid, but the Lord calls Saul his chosen vessel to carry his name to Gentiles, kings and Israel (9:15). The worst enemy becomes the chief messenger, and later Paul calls himself the least of the apostles for this past.

insights.title: Brother Saul
insights.body: Ananias's first words to the man who came to arrest him are Brother Saul (9:17). Grace shows in a greeting before any lecture.

insights.title: Down the wall in a basket
insights.body: Saul escapes Damascus by night, lowered through the wall in a basket (9:25). Paul later recalls this humiliating exit as one of the things he could boast about in weakness.

insights.title: Tabitha, get up
insights.body: Peter sends everyone out, prays, and says, Tabitha, get up (9:40), much as Jesus said to Jairus's daughter. Elijah and Elisha also raised the dead after praying alone.

insights.title: The person you fear
insights.body: Ananias was asked to go to a man known for harming believers. Is there someone you've written off as beyond God's reach?

10.summary: An angel tells the Roman centurion Cornelius to send for Peter; Peter sees a vision of unclean animals, goes to Cornelius's house, preaches, and the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentile listeners, who are baptized.
10.lookfor: Notice how both men are prepared by God before they meet, and what Peter learns from the vision.

names.name: Cornelius
names.gloss: A Roman centurion in Caesarea who feared God.

names.name: Caesarea
names.gloss: The Roman capital of Judea, a port built by Herod the Great.

names.name: Simon
names.gloss: A tanner in Joppa with whom Peter stayed.

insights.title: A God-fearer
insights.body: Cornelius is devout, prays and gives to the poor but isn't a full convert (10:2). Such God-fearers attended synagogues and worshiped Israel's God without circumcision, and they were often the first to believe.

insights.title: A tanner's house
insights.body: Peter lodges with a tanner (10:6), whose work with dead animals made him ritually unclean to many. Peter is already bending the rules before the vision comes.

insights.title: Three times
insights.body: The sheet comes down three times, and Peter refuses three times (10:16). Peter, who denied Jesus three times and was restored three times, learns slowly but surely.

insights.title: Food and people
insights.body: The vision is about food, but Peter applies it to people: God has shown him not to call any person unholy or unclean (10:28). Jews avoided entering Gentile homes, and food laws helped keep them apart.

insights.title: No respecter of persons
insights.body: Peter realizes God doesn't show favoritism (10:34). The phrase means literally not receiving faces, judging by appearance or rank. The law said the same of God.

insights.title: The Gentile Pentecost
insights.body: While Peter is still speaking, the Spirit falls on the Gentiles, and they speak in tongues (10:44-46). The Jewish believers are amazed: God gave them the same gift he gave us, before baptism or circumcision.

insights.title: Who is unclean to you?
insights.body: Peter had to unlearn lifelong instincts about who was acceptable. What group do you instinctively keep at a distance?

11.summary: Peter defends baptizing Gentiles to the Jerusalem church, which praises God; in Antioch Gentiles believe in large numbers, Barnabas brings Saul, the disciples are first called Christians, and they send famine relief to Judea.
11.lookfor: Notice how Peter answers criticism by simply telling what happened, and the first mixed church at Antioch.

names.name: Phoenicia
names.gloss: The coastal region north of Galilee, around Tyre and Sidon.

names.name: Antioch
names.gloss: Antioch in Syria, third city of the Roman Empire.

names.name: Cyrene
names.gloss: A city in North Africa, in modern Libya.

names.name: Agabus
names.gloss: A prophet from Jerusalem who foretold a famine.

names.name: Claudius
names.gloss: Roman emperor from AD 41 to 54.

insights.title: You ate with them
insights.body: The complaint against Peter is that he went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them (11:3). Sharing a table meant acceptance, which is why it was the sharpest test.

insights.title: Who was I?
insights.body: Peter retells everything and ends by asking who he was, to withstand God (11:17). The critics fall silent and glorify God (11:18). The early church changed its mind when it saw God at work.

insights.title: Antioch
insights.body: Unnamed believers from Cyprus and Cyrene first preach to Greeks in Antioch (11:20). This mixed church of Jews and Gentiles becomes the base for Paul's journeys.

insights.title: Christians
insights.body: The disciples are first called Christians at Antioch (11:26), probably a nickname from outsiders meaning Christ's people. The word appears only three times in the New Testament.

insights.title: Barnabas looks for Saul
insights.body: Barnabas sees God's grace in Antioch, is glad, and goes to Tarsus to find Saul (11:23-25). Again the encourager opens the door for Saul.

insights.title: Famine under Claudius
insights.body: Agabus predicts a great famine, which happened in the days of Claudius (11:28). Roman writers record food shortages in various regions during his reign. The Antioch church sends relief to Judea, each according to his ability.

insights.title: Changing your mind
insights.body: The Jerusalem believers were critical until they heard the full story. When did hearing someone out change your view?

12.summary: Herod kills James and arrests Peter; while the church prays, an angel leads Peter out of prison to a house where the girl Rhoda forgets to open the door; Herod later dies after accepting worship as a god.
12.lookfor: Notice the church praying, then not believing their prayer was answered, and how the chapter contrasts Herod's end with the word's growth.

names.name: Herod
names.gloss: Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, king of Judea AD 41–44.

names.name: James
names.gloss: James son of Zebedee, John's brother, the first apostle killed.

names.name: Mary
names.gloss: Mother of John Mark, whose house was a meeting place.

names.name: Rhoda
names.gloss: A servant girl who answered Peter's knock.

names.name: Blastus
names.gloss: Herod's chamberlain.

insights.title: James killed, Peter freed
insights.body: James is killed with the sword (12:2), and Peter is miraculously freed. Acts doesn't explain why one was spared and one wasn't; faithfulness doesn't guarantee escape.

insights.title: Four squads
insights.body: Peter is guarded by four squads of four soldiers, chained between two (12:4-6). Herod is taking no chances after the apostles' earlier escape.

insights.title: Peter asleep
insights.body: The night before his likely execution, Peter is sound asleep, and the angel has to strike his side to wake him (12:7). The psalmist could lie down and sleep in peace because the Lord kept him safe.

insights.title: Rhoda at the gate
insights.body: Rhoda is so glad to hear Peter's voice that she runs to tell the others without opening the gate (12:14). The praying church tells her she's mad. One of Acts' funniest scenes.

insights.title: The voice of a god
insights.body: The crowd shouts that Herod's voice is a god's, and he is struck down because he didn't give God the glory (12:22-23). The historian Josephus also describes Agrippa's sudden death at Caesarea after being hailed as more than human.

insights.title: But the word grew
insights.body: Herod, who killed James, dies eaten by worms, but the word of God grew and multiplied (12:24). The persecutor ends; the message goes on.

insights.title: Surprised by answers
insights.body: The church prayed earnestly for Peter, then couldn't believe he was at the door. When has God answered a prayer you didn't really expect him to?

13.summary: The Spirit sends Barnabas and Saul from Antioch; on Cyprus a sorcerer is blinded and the proconsul believes; in Pisidian Antioch Paul preaches in the synagogue, and when many Jews reject the message, he turns to the Gentiles.
13.lookfor: Notice that Saul begins to be called Paul and takes the lead, and the pattern of synagogue first, then Gentiles.

names.name: Manaen
names.gloss: A prophet or teacher at Antioch, brought up with Herod Antipas.

names.name: Seleucia
names.gloss: Antioch's port on the Mediterranean.

names.name: Salamis
names.gloss: A port city on the east coast of Cyprus.

names.name: Paphos
names.gloss: The Roman capital of Cyprus, on the west coast.

names.name: Elymas
names.gloss: A sorcerer, also called Bar Jesus, who opposed Paul.

names.name: Sergius Paulus
names.gloss: The Roman proconsul of Cyprus.

names.name: Perga
names.gloss: A city in Pamphylia, on the south coast of Asia Minor.

names.name: Pisidia
names.gloss: A region in south-central Asia Minor.

insights.title: A mixed leadership
insights.body: Antioch's leaders include Simeon called Niger (meaning black), Lucius of Cyrene in Africa, and Manaen, who grew up with a king (13:1). The church's leaders were as varied as its members.

insights.title: Saul who is also Paul
insights.body: Saul is called Paul from 13:9. As a Roman citizen, he likely had both names all along; from here he uses his Roman one in a Gentile world, and the order shifts from Barnabas and Saul to Paul and Barnabas.

insights.title: Mark goes home
insights.body: John Mark leaves them at Perga and returns to Jerusalem (13:13). Acts gives no reason, but it later causes a sharp split between Paul and Barnabas.

insights.title: Synagogue first
insights.body: In each city Paul goes first to the synagogue, where Jews and God-fearers already know the Scriptures (13:14-16). Synagogue leaders often invited visiting teachers to speak after the readings.

insights.title: The holy blessings of David
insights.body: Paul's sermon traces Israel's story to David, quotes Psalm 2's words to the Son, and the promise of David's blessings (13:33-34), showing Jesus as David's heir who did not see decay.

insights.title: A light for the Gentiles
insights.body: When many Jews reject them, Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, quoting Isaiah's call to be a light for the nations (13:47). Simeon had said the same of the infant Jesus.

insights.title: Shaking off the dust
insights.body: Driven out, they shake the dust off their feet, yet the disciples are filled with joy and the Holy Spirit (13:51-52). How do you respond when people reject what matters most to you?

14.summary: Paul and Barnabas preach in Iconium, Lystra and Derbe; at Lystra a healing leads crowds to worship them as gods, then Paul is stoned and left for dead; they return, strengthen the churches, appoint elders and report back to Antioch.
14.lookfor: Notice how Paul speaks to pagans who don't know the Scriptures, and the courage of going back to cities that attacked them.

names.name: Iconium
names.gloss: A city in south-central Asia Minor, modern Konya.

names.name: Lystra
names.gloss: A Roman colony in Lycaonia, later Timothy's home.

names.name: Derbe
names.gloss: A town in Lycaonia, the farthest point of this journey.

names.name: Lycaonia
names.gloss: A region of south-central Asia Minor with its own language.

names.name: Attalia
names.gloss: A port on the south coast, modern Antalya.

insights.title: Gods in human form
insights.body: The crowd names Barnabas and Paul after two gods, giving Paul the messenger god's name because he does the talking (14:12). A local legend told of these gods visiting the region in human form unrecognized, and the people may not want to make that mistake again.

insights.title: Tearing their clothes
insights.body: Hearing in their own language that they are being worshiped, Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes (14:14), a Jewish sign of horror at blasphemy, and rush in shouting that they are only human.

insights.title: Preaching to pagans
insights.body: To people with no Bible, Paul starts with creation: the living God who made heaven and earth gave rain and fruitful seasons (14:15-17). He meets them where they are, as he will again in Athens.

insights.title: Back into the city
insights.body: Paul is stoned, dragged out and left for dead, then gets up and goes back into the city (14:19-20). Years later he lists being stoned once among his sufferings.

insights.title: Many afflictions
insights.body: They tell the new believers that we must enter God's kingdom through many afflictions (14:22). The word for affliction is thlipsis, pressure or crushing, not a sign that something has gone wrong.

insights.title: A door of faith
insights.body: Back in Antioch they report that God opened a door of faith to the Gentiles (14:27). How Gentiles would be received was about to become the church's biggest question.

insights.title: Strengthening others
insights.body: Paul and Barnabas went back to strengthen young believers in dangerous cities (14:21-22). Who could you encourage to keep going this week?

15.summary: When some insist Gentile believers must be circumcised, the apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem, hear Peter, Barnabas and Paul, and James proposes a letter freeing Gentiles from the law with a few requests; later Paul and Barnabas part over Mark.
15.lookfor: Notice the question at stake, how the council reaches a decision, and the sharp disagreement at the end.

names.name: James
names.gloss: The brother of Jesus, leader of the Jerusalem church.

names.name: Simeon
names.gloss: The Hebrew form of Simon, used here for Peter.

names.name: Silas
names.gloss: A leader in Jerusalem who became Paul's travel companion.

names.name: Barsabbas
names.gloss: Judas called Barsabbas, sent with Silas to carry the letter.

names.name: Cilicia
names.gloss: The region in southeast Asia Minor around Tarsus.

insights.title: The question
insights.body: Men from Judea teach that unless you are circumcised according to Moses, you can't be saved (15:1). Must Gentiles become Jews to follow Jesus? The whole future of the church hangs on the answer.

insights.title: A yoke we couldn't bear
insights.body: Peter calls the law a yoke that neither our fathers nor we were able to bear and says we are saved through grace just as they are (15:10-11). Jew and Gentile stand on the same ground.

insights.title: David's fallen tent
insights.body: James quotes Amos: God will rebuild David's fallen tent, so that the rest of humanity and all the Gentiles may seek the Lord (15:16-17). The prophets expected the nations to join Israel's restored kingdom.

insights.title: Four requests
insights.body: Gentiles are asked to avoid food offered to idols, sexual immorality, what is strangled, and blood (15:20, 15:29). These echo rules in Leviticus for foreigners living in Israel and made shared meals with Jewish believers possible.

insights.title: It seemed good
insights.body: The letter says it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us (15:28). The decision came through Scripture, testimony, debate and the Spirit's leading together, a model for hard questions.

insights.title: A sharp contention
insights.body: Paul and Barnabas disagree so sharply over taking Mark that they part ways (15:39). Even good leaders fall out. Years later Paul calls Mark useful to him.

insights.title: Extra burdens
insights.body: The council refused to add requirements beyond faith in Jesus. Are there unwritten rules you expect others to keep before you accept them?

16.summary: Timothy joins Paul and Silas; a vision calls them to Macedonia, where Lydia believes in Philippi, a slave girl is freed from a spirit, Paul and Silas are beaten and jailed, sing at midnight, and the jailer's household is baptized.
16.lookfor: Notice the closed doors before the open one, the three very different people who believe in Philippi, and the shift to "we" in verse 10.

names.name: Timothy
names.gloss: A young believer from Lystra, son of a Jewish mother and Greek father.

names.name: Bithynia
names.gloss: A region in northwest Asia Minor.

names.name: Troas
names.gloss: A port on the Aegean coast near ancient Troy.

names.name: Macedonia
names.gloss: The Roman province in northern Greece.

names.name: Philippi
names.gloss: A Roman colony in Macedonia, named after Philip of Macedon.

names.name: Lydia
names.gloss: A dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, the first convert in Europe.

names.name: Thyatira
names.gloss: A city in Asia Minor famous for its dyes.

insights.title: Closed doors
insights.body: The Spirit forbids them to speak in Asia and won't let them enter Bithynia (16:6-7). Only then comes the vision of a man of Macedonia calling for help (16:9). Guidance often came through blocked plans.

insights.title: Enter "we"
insights.body: At 16:10 the story switches to we. Many take this as the author joining Paul at Troas, and the we sections that follow read like a traveller's diary.

insights.title: A place of prayer by the river
insights.body: Paul looks for a place of prayer by the river (16:13). A synagogue needed ten Jewish men; Philippi apparently lacked them, so women met outdoors, and the first church in Europe begins with them.

insights.title: Three converts
insights.body: A wealthy businesswoman, an exploited slave girl, and a Roman jailer (16:14-34): the Philippian church starts with people from very different worlds. Paul later writes this church his warmest letter.

insights.title: Songs at midnight
insights.body: Beaten and in stocks, Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight while the prisoners listen (16:25). Then an earthquake opens every door.

insights.title: Why the jailer drew his sword
insights.body: A Roman guard who lost prisoners could face their punishment himself, so he prepares to kill himself (16:27). Paul shouts that all are there, and the jailer asks what he must do to be saved.

insights.title: Singing in the dark
insights.body: Paul and Silas worshiped before anything changed. What would singing at midnight look like in your hard situation?

17.summary: In Thessalonica a riot drives Paul out; in Beroea people examine the Scriptures daily; in Athens Paul, troubled by the idols, debates in the marketplace and speaks to the Areopagus about the unknown God.
17.lookfor: Notice how Paul's approach changes with his audience, and his starting point in Athens.

names.name: Thessalonica
names.gloss: The capital of Macedonia, a busy port.

names.name: Jason
names.gloss: Paul's host in Thessalonica, dragged before the rulers.

names.name: Beroea
names.gloss: A town in Macedonia west of Thessalonica.

names.name: Athens
names.gloss: The famous Greek city of philosophy and art.

names.name: Epicurean
names.gloss: Followers of Epicurus, who taught that the gods are distant and pleasure, meaning peace of mind, is the goal.

names.name: Stoic
names.gloss: Philosophers who taught living by reason in line with a divine order.

names.name: Areopagus
names.gloss: Mars' Hill, and the council of Athens that met there.

names.name: Damaris
names.gloss: A woman in Athens who believed.

insights.title: Turned the world upside down
insights.body: The accusers say these men have turned the world upside down and claim another king, Jesus (17:6-7). Opponents understood the political sting of calling Jesus king.

insights.title: More noble
insights.body: The Beroeans are more noble than the Thessalonians: they receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily to see if these things are so (17:11). Eager and careful go together.

insights.title: A babbler
insights.body: Some philosophers call Paul a babbler (17:18), literally a seed-picker, a bird pecking at scraps, someone who picks up bits of ideas. Athens loved novelty.

insights.title: The unknown God
insights.body: Paul starts from an altar inscribed to an unknown God (17:23). He doesn't quote Scripture to people who don't know it but begins with their own longings and works toward the resurrection.

insights.title: Quoting their poets
insights.body: Paul quotes Greek poets: in him we live, move and have our being, and we are his offspring (17:28). The second line comes from Aratus, a poet from Paul's own region. Truth found in their poets points to the Creator.

insights.title: Some mocked, some joined
insights.body: At the mention of resurrection some mock, some want to hear more, and a few believe, including Dionysius, a council member, and Damaris (17:32-34). A mixed result, but a real one.

insights.title: Where to start
insights.body: Paul began with what Athenians already wondered about. What questions do the people around you already ask that could open a conversation about God?

18.summary: In Corinth Paul works with Aquila and Priscilla making tents, preaches for eighteen months after a vision tells him not to fear, and is protected when Gallio dismisses the charges; Apollos is taught more accurately in Ephesus.
18.lookfor: Notice Paul working a trade, the vision at a discouraging moment, and how Priscilla and Aquila help Apollos.

names.name: Corinth
names.gloss: A wealthy port city in southern Greece, capital of Achaia.

names.name: Aquila
names.gloss: A Jewish tentmaker from Pontus, Priscilla's husband.

names.name: Priscilla
names.gloss: Aquila's wife, a teacher and co-worker of Paul.

names.name: Crispus
names.gloss: The synagogue ruler in Corinth who believed.

names.name: Gallio
names.gloss: Proconsul of Achaia, brother of the philosopher Seneca.

names.name: Sosthenes
names.gloss: A synagogue ruler beaten before Gallio.

names.name: Apollos
names.gloss: An eloquent Jewish teacher from Alexandria.

insights.title: Claudius expels the Jews
insights.body: Aquila and Priscilla came from Italy because Claudius ordered all Jews out of Rome (18:2). The Roman writer Suetonius mentions this expulsion over disturbances about one Chrestus, possibly a garbled reference to Christ.

insights.title: Tentmakers
insights.body: Paul works with them at their shared trade, tentmaking or leatherwork (18:3). He supported himself so no one could say he preached for money.

insights.title: Do not be afraid
insights.body: The Lord tells Paul in a vision not to be afraid but to keep speaking, for he has many people in this city (18:9-10). Paul later admits he came to Corinth in weakness, fear and trembling, and God had spoken the same courage to Joshua.

insights.title: Gallio's seat
insights.body: An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio's term as proconsul to about AD 51–52, one of the firmest dates for Paul's life. Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about words and names (18:15), which effectively protects the church.

insights.title: Priscilla first
insights.body: Priscilla is often named before her husband (18:18, 18:26), which was unusual and may mean she was the more prominent of the two. Together they take Apollos aside and explain the way of God more accurately.

insights.title: Apollos
insights.body: Apollos is mighty in the Scriptures but knows only John's baptism (18:24-25). Taught privately and kindly, he goes on to strengthen the believers in Achaia.

insights.title: Correcting gently
insights.body: Priscilla and Aquila corrected a gifted teacher privately, not publicly. How do you handle it when someone's understanding is incomplete?

19.summary: In Ephesus Paul baptizes disciples of John, teaches for two years, and God does extraordinary miracles; magicians burn their scrolls, and Demetrius the silversmith stirs a riot in the theater over the goddess Artemis.
19.lookfor: Notice the costly bonfire of magic books, and what really drives the riot.

names.name: Ephesus
names.gloss: The leading city of the province of Asia, home of a great temple of Artemis.

names.name: Tyrannus
names.gloss: Owner of a lecture hall where Paul taught daily.

names.name: Sceva
names.gloss: A Jewish chief priest whose seven sons tried to use Jesus' name as a spell.

names.name: Demetrius
names.gloss: A silversmith who made shrines of Artemis.

names.name: Artemis
names.gloss: The goddess of Ephesus, worshiped across Asia.

names.name: Aristarchus
names.gloss: A Macedonian from Thessalonica, Paul's companion.

insights.title: Into John's baptism
insights.body: Paul meets about twelve disciples who know only John's baptism and haven't heard of the Holy Spirit (19:2-3). Baptized in Jesus' name, they receive the Spirit, completing what John pointed to.

insights.title: Handkerchiefs and aprons
insights.body: Handkerchiefs and aprons that touched Paul's skin heal the sick (19:12). These were likely the sweatbands and work aprons of his trade; God worked through ordinary things.

insights.title: Jesus I know
insights.body: The evil spirit answers the sons of Sceva that it knows Jesus and Paul, but asks who they are (19:15). Jesus' name isn't a magic formula for people who don't know him.

insights.title: The burning of the books
insights.body: New believers burn their magic books worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (19:19), a fortune. Ephesus was famous for magical texts called Ephesian letters.

insights.title: Money behind the riot
insights.body: Demetrius warns his fellow craftsmen that their trade and the goddess's honor are at risk (19:25-27). Profit is the real motive; religion is the slogan. The crowd shouts for two hours, most not knowing why they've gathered (19:32).

insights.title: Two years in Ephesus
insights.body: Paul teaches daily in the hall of Tyrannus for two years, so all who lived in Asia heard the word (19:10). The churches of Colossae and others in Revelation likely began in this period.

insights.title: What's worth burning?
insights.body: The Ephesians destroyed valuable things that tied them to their old life. Is there anything you hold on to that pulls you away from God?

20.summary: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, raises Eutychus after a long sermon in Troas, and at Miletus gives a moving farewell to the Ephesian elders, urging them to shepherd God's flock.
20.lookfor: Notice how Paul describes his own ministry, his warning about wolves, and the tears at parting.

names.name: Eutychus
names.gloss: A young man in Troas who fell from a window; his name means fortunate.

names.name: Assos
names.gloss: A port south of Troas.

names.name: Mitylene
names.gloss: The main city of the island of Lesbos.

names.name: Miletus
names.gloss: A port about 30 miles south of Ephesus.

names.name: Sopater
names.gloss: A believer from Beroea who travelled with Paul.

insights.title: The first day of the week
insights.body: The believers gather on the first day of the week to break bread (20:7), one of the earliest signs of Christians meeting on Sunday, the day of the resurrection.

insights.title: A long sermon
insights.body: Paul talks until midnight, and Eutychus, sitting in a window, sinks into a deep sleep and falls three floors (20:9). Paul raises him, eats, and keeps talking until dawn. Acts tells it with a straight face.

insights.title: Why a farewell
insights.body: Paul believes he won't see them again, since the Spirit warns of chains and afflictions in every city (20:23-25). His speech is like a last testament to leaders who must carry on without him.

insights.title: Overseers and shepherds
insights.body: Paul tells the elders the Holy Spirit made them overseers to shepherd God's church, bought with his own blood (20:28). Elder, overseer and shepherd all describe the same leaders here.

insights.title: More blessed to give
insights.body: Paul quotes Jesus: it is more blessed to give than to receive (20:35). The saying appears in no Gospel, a reminder that more of Jesus' words were remembered than were written down.

insights.title: Wolves
insights.body: Paul warns that fierce wolves will come in among them, and some will rise from their own number (20:29-30). Years later his letters to Timothy in Ephesus deal with exactly this.

insights.title: Finishing well
insights.body: Paul says he doesn't count his life dear, so long as he finishes his course with joy (20:24). What would finishing well look like for you?

21.summary: Despite warnings from believers and the prophet Agabus, Paul goes to Jerusalem; to calm rumors he joins a purification rite in the temple, but a mob seizes him and the Roman commander arrests him, and Paul asks to speak to the crowd.
21.lookfor: Notice the repeated warnings and Paul's resolve, and the rumor that sparks the riot.

names.name: Tyre
names.gloss: A Phoenician port north of Galilee.

names.name: Ptolemais
names.gloss: A coastal city, Old Testament Acco.

names.name: Agabus
names.gloss: The prophet who had foretold famine, now foretelling Paul's arrest.

names.name: Mnason
names.gloss: An early disciple from Cyprus who hosted Paul's group.

names.name: Trophimus
names.gloss: A Gentile believer from Ephesus.

insights.title: Philip's daughters
insights.body: Paul stays with Philip the evangelist, who has four unmarried daughters who prophesied (21:9). Joel's promise about sons and daughters prophesying is lived out.

insights.title: Agabus and the belt
insights.body: Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul's belt to show what will happen in Jerusalem (21:11). Old Testament prophets often acted out their messages.

insights.title: Like his Lord
insights.body: Paul says he is ready not only to be bound but to die in Jerusalem for the Lord Jesus' name (21:13). Like Jesus, he sets his face toward Jerusalem knowing what awaits him.

insights.title: Why Paul joined the vow
insights.body: Rumors say Paul teaches Jews to abandon Moses, so the elders ask him to pay for four men's purification vows (21:21-24). Paul was free from the law but willing to keep it to win Jews.

insights.title: The forbidden court
insights.body: The mob thinks Paul brought Trophimus, a Gentile, into the temple (21:28-29). Stone notices warned Gentiles against entering the inner courts on pain of death, and archaeologists have found two of them.

insights.title: Arrested
insights.body: Roman soldiers rescue Paul from the beating, and the crowd shouts, Away with him (21:36), as they once shouted about Jesus. The last quarter of Acts follows Paul as a prisoner.

insights.title: Warnings and calling
insights.body: Loving friends begged Paul not to go, and he went anyway, convinced of God's call. How do you weigh wise counsel against a strong sense of calling?

22.summary: Speaking in Aramaic from the barracks steps, Paul tells the crowd how he persecuted the Way and met Jesus near Damascus; when he says he was sent to the Gentiles, the crowd erupts, and he avoids flogging by revealing he is a Roman citizen.
22.lookfor: Notice how Paul presents himself as a zealous Jew, and the exact word that sets the crowd off again.

names.name: Gamaliel
names.gloss: The respected Pharisee teacher at whose feet Paul studied.

names.name: Tarsus
names.gloss: Paul's birthplace, in Cilicia.

names.name: Ananias
names.gloss: The devout believer in Damascus who restored Paul's sight.

names.name: Stephen
names.gloss: The martyr whose death Paul approved.

insights.title: In the Hebrew language
insights.body: When Paul speaks in Hebrew, probably Aramaic, the everyday language of Judea, the crowd goes even quieter (22:2). He speaks to them as one of their own.

insights.title: Zealous as you are
insights.body: Paul says he was zealous for God, as they all are today (22:3). He doesn't condemn their zeal; he once shared it and knows how it can be misdirected.

insights.title: The story told again
insights.body: This is the second of three tellings of Paul's conversion (chapters 9, 22, 26). Each one adds details suited to its audience; here Paul stresses Ananias's devotion to the law.

insights.title: The word Gentiles
insights.body: The crowd listens until Paul says the Lord sent him far away to the Gentiles (22:21-22). For many, the idea that Gentiles could share Israel's hope without becoming Jews was intolerable.

insights.title: Born a citizen
insights.body: Flogging a Roman citizen without trial was illegal. The commander bought his citizenship for a great price, but Paul was born a citizen (22:28), a higher status.

insights.title: Your witness
insights.body: Ananias told Paul he would be a witness to all people of what he had seen and heard (22:15). Paul's own story becomes his main message in these final chapters.

insights.title: Your own story
insights.body: Paul often shared his testimony rather than an argument. How would you tell the story of how you came to faith, or where you are now?

23.summary: Before the council Paul divides Pharisees and Sadducees over the resurrection; the Lord tells him he will testify in Rome; his nephew uncovers a plot to kill him, and the commander sends him under heavy guard to Governor Felix in Caesarea.
23.lookfor: Notice the Lord's encouragement at night, and the small part played by Paul's nephew.

names.name: Ananias
names.gloss: The high priest, known for greed and violence; not the earlier Ananias.

names.name: Pharisees
names.gloss: The party strict about the law, who believed in resurrection and angels.

names.name: Sadducees
names.gloss: The priestly party who denied resurrection, angels and spirits.

names.name: Claudius Lysias
names.gloss: The Roman commander in Jerusalem.

names.name: Felix
names.gloss: Antonius Felix, Roman governor of Judea about AD 52–59.

names.name: Antipatris
names.gloss: A town on the road from Jerusalem to Caesarea, built by Herod.

insights.title: You whitewashed wall
insights.body: Struck on the mouth on the high priest's order, Paul calls him a whitewashed wall, then apologizes when told who he is, quoting the law against speaking evil of a ruler (23:3-5).

insights.title: Why Paul raised the resurrection
insights.body: Paul says he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection (23:6). It's a clever move, splitting the council, but also true: the resurrection was the heart of his message.

insights.title: Take courage
insights.body: The night after the uproar, the Lord stands by Paul and tells him to take courage: he must testify in Rome too (23:11). The promise carries Paul through two years of prison and a shipwreck.

insights.title: The oath not to eat
insights.body: More than forty men bind themselves under a curse not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul (23:12-13). Such vows were serious, though rabbis allowed release from impossible ones; we never learn what happened to them.

insights.title: Four hundred seventy men
insights.body: The commander sends 200 soldiers, 70 horsemen and 200 spearmen (23:23) to guard one prisoner overnight. Rome took the protection of a citizen seriously, and the commander wanted no trouble.

insights.title: Protected by Rome
insights.body: The Roman letter says Paul has done nothing worthy of death or chains (23:29). Like Pilate with Jesus, officials keep finding Paul innocent, a theme Luke stresses.

insights.title: Small parts
insights.body: Paul's nephew, unnamed, saved his life by reporting what he overheard. What small act of courage might matter more than you think?

24.summary: Before Felix, the lawyer Tertullus accuses Paul of stirring riots; Paul calmly answers that he worships the God of his fathers and hopes in the resurrection; Felix delays, talks with Paul often hoping for a bribe, and leaves him in prison two years.
24.lookfor: Notice the flattery in the charge, Paul's calm defense, and what makes Felix afraid.

names.name: Tertullus
names.gloss: A professional speaker hired to accuse Paul.

names.name: Nazarenes
names.gloss: A name for Jesus' followers, after Nazareth.

names.name: Drusilla
names.gloss: Felix's Jewish wife, daughter of Herod Agrippa I.

names.name: Festus
names.gloss: Porcius Festus, who succeeded Felix as governor.

insights.title: Flattery
insights.body: Tertullus praises Felix for much peace and reforms (24:2-3). The historian Tacitus said Felix wielded the power of a king with the mind of a slave, and his rule was marked by unrest. The praise is formula.

insights.title: A sect
insights.body: Paul is called a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes (24:5). Paul replies that he worships according to the Way, which they call a sect (24:14). The word hairesis later came to mean heresy.

insights.title: A clear conscience
insights.body: Paul says he strives to have a conscience void of offense toward God and people (24:16). His defense rests on a life lived openly.

insights.title: Why Felix was afraid
insights.body: As Paul talks about righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, Felix becomes afraid (24:25). He had taken Drusilla from her first husband; the topics hit close to home.

insights.title: A convenient time
insights.body: Felix sends Paul away until he has a convenient time (24:25), and keeps meeting him, hoping for money (24:26). The convenient time never comes. Delay can become a decision.

insights.title: Two years lost?
insights.body: Paul waits two years in Caesarea (24:27). Some suggest Luke gathered material for his Gospel during this time in Judea, though Acts doesn't say.

insights.title: Putting off
insights.body: Felix heard the truth, felt its weight, and postponed. What have you been putting off until a more convenient time?

25.summary: The new governor Festus hears the case; to avoid being handed to Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar; King Agrippa and Bernice visit, and Festus arranges for them to hear Paul because he has no charge to write.
25.lookfor: Notice why Paul appeals to Caesar, and how Festus describes the dispute to Agrippa.

names.name: Festus
names.gloss: Porcius Festus, governor of Judea about AD 59–62.

names.name: Caesar
names.gloss: The emperor, at this time Nero.

names.name: Agrippa
names.gloss: Herod Agrippa II, great-grandson of Herod the Great, ruler of territories north of Galilee.

names.name: Bernice
names.gloss: Agrippa's sister and companion.

insights.title: The appeal to Caesar
insights.body: When Festus suggests a trial in Jerusalem, where an ambush awaits, Paul uses his right as a citizen: I appeal to Caesar (25:11). It also fulfills the Lord's word that he would testify in Rome.

insights.title: Caesar was Nero
insights.body: The Caesar here is Nero, who in his early years was seen as reasonable. Within a few years he would turn violently on Christians in Rome.

insights.title: One Jesus who was dead
insights.body: Festus sums up the dispute as being about their religion and one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive (25:19). An outsider's summary that gets the center exactly right.

insights.title: Great pomp
insights.body: Agrippa and Bernice enter with great pomp, with commanders and the city's leading men (25:23). The prisoner in chains will be the one with the message that matters.

insights.title: Before kings
insights.body: Jesus told Saul he would carry his name before Gentiles and kings, and told his disciples they'd be brought before kings for his sake (Luke 21:12). Here it happens.

insights.title: Nothing to write
insights.body: Festus admits he has nothing certain to write to the emperor (25:26). Again a Roman official can find no crime.

insights.title: Using your rights
insights.body: Paul used his legal rights wisely, without bitterness. How can you use what you've been given, status, rights, connections, for God's purposes?

26.summary: Before Agrippa, Paul tells his story a third time: his zeal as a Pharisee, his vision of Jesus and his call to open Gentiles' eyes; Festus says he is mad, Agrippa jokes about becoming a Christian, and all agree Paul could have been freed.
26.lookfor: Notice the new details of Jesus' words, and Paul's personal appeal to Agrippa.

names.name: Agrippa
names.gloss: Herod Agrippa II, an expert in Jewish customs.

names.name: Festus
names.gloss: The Roman governor.

names.name: Damascus
names.gloss: The Syrian city where Paul met Jesus.

insights.title: The hope of the promise
insights.body: Paul says he is on trial for hope in the promise God made to the fathers (26:6). Why should anyone think it incredible that God raises the dead? (26:8).

insights.title: Kicking against the goads
insights.body: Jesus tells Saul it is hard for him to kick against the goads (26:14). A goad was a pointed stick for driving oxen; an ox that kicked only hurt itself. It was a Greek proverb for fighting the gods.

insights.title: Open their eyes
insights.body: Jesus sends Paul to open eyes and turn people from darkness to light (26:18), the mission of Isaiah's servant. Paul, struck blind and given sight, is sent to do the same for others.

insights.title: Not done in a corner
insights.body: Paul tells Agrippa that none of this was done in a corner (26:26). Jesus' death and the church's growth were public events Agrippa would have known about.

insights.title: Almost persuaded?
insights.body: Agrippa asks if Paul thinks he can make him a Christian so quickly (26:28), probably with irony. Paul answers that he wishes everyone listening were as he is, except for these chains (26:29).

insights.title: Could have been freed
insights.body: Agrippa says Paul could have been set free if he hadn't appealed to Caesar (26:32). His appeal, which seemed a setback, is God's way to Rome.

insights.title: Not disobedient
insights.body: Paul says he was not disobedient to the heavenly vision (26:19). What has God shown you that you're still deciding whether to obey?

27.summary: Paul sails for Rome as a prisoner; against his advice the ship leaves Crete, a violent storm drives it for two weeks, an angel promises all will survive, and the ship runs aground and breaks up, but all 276 aboard reach land.
27.lookfor: Notice how Paul, the prisoner, becomes the calm leader on board, and the vivid seafaring details.

names.name: Julius
names.gloss: A centurion of the Augustan band who treated Paul kindly.

names.name: Sidon
names.gloss: A Phoenician port north of Tyre.

names.name: Myra
names.gloss: A port in Lycia, southwest Asia Minor.

names.name: Crete
names.gloss: A large Greek island south of the Aegean.

names.name: Fair Havens
names.gloss: A small harbor on Crete's south coast.

insights.title: After the Fast
insights.body: The voyage is dangerous because the Fast had already gone by (27:9), meaning the Day of Atonement in autumn. Sailing the Mediterranean after mid-September was risky and stopped entirely in winter.

insights.title: Seafaring detail
insights.body: Luke describes undergirding the ship with ropes, lowering the gear, throwing cargo and tackle overboard and taking soundings (27:17-28). Sailors have praised the passage as one of the most accurate ancient accounts of a voyage.

insights.title: Paul takes charge
insights.body: After days without sun or stars, when all hope is lost (27:20), the prisoner stands up and tells everyone to take courage, because an angel has promised no one will die.

insights.title: Jonah reversed
insights.body: Jonah, fleeing God, slept through a storm and had to be thrown overboard to save the crew. Paul, obeying God, is the reason everyone aboard is saved (27:24).

insights.title: Breaking bread
insights.body: Before dawn Paul takes bread, gives thanks before them all, breaks it and eats (27:35), urging them to eat for their survival. The words echo the Last Supper, though this is an ordinary meal among pagans.

insights.title: All safe to land
insights.body: Soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but the centurion stops them to save Paul, and everyone reaches land, some swimming, some on planks (27:42-44). God's promise holds exactly.

insights.title: Courage in the storm
insights.body: Paul's peace came from a promise, not from the weather. What promise of God do you lean on when everything feels out of control?

28.summary: On Malta Paul survives a viper bite and heals many; he reaches Rome, meets the Jewish leaders, some of whom believe, and for two years he lives under guard in his own rented house, preaching the kingdom boldly and without hindrance.
28.lookfor: Notice the warm welcome by believers on the road, Paul's last quotation of Isaiah, and how the book ends.

names.name: Malta
names.gloss: An island south of Sicily.

names.name: Publius
names.gloss: The chief official of Malta, whose father Paul healed.

names.name: Syracuse
names.gloss: The main city of Sicily.

names.name: Puteoli
names.gloss: A port near Naples, where grain ships for Rome unloaded.

names.name: Rome
names.gloss: The capital of the empire.

insights.title: Justice won't let him live
insights.body: When the viper fastens on Paul's hand, the islanders say Justice, a goddess, won't let a murderer live (28:4). When he doesn't die, they change their minds and call him a god.

insights.title: The Twin Brothers
insights.body: The ship to Italy bears the figurehead of the Twin Brothers (28:11), Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus and patrons of sailors. Luke notes it without comment: the true protector of this voyage was someone else.

insights.title: He took courage
insights.body: Believers walk out from Rome to meet Paul on the road, and seeing them, he thanks God and takes courage (28:15). Even Paul needed encouragement from friends.

insights.title: Isaiah's hard word
insights.body: Paul closes with Isaiah: they will hear but not understand, see but not perceive (28:26-27). Jesus used the same words about his parables. Rejection was foreseen, but the message goes on to the Gentiles.

insights.title: An open ending
insights.body: Acts ends with Paul preaching freely in Rome (28:31), without telling us what happened at his trial. Many think the story stops there on purpose: the gospel has reached the capital, and the story continues with every reader.

insights.title: Unhindered
insights.body: The last word of Acts in Greek is akōlytōs, unhindered (28:31). Paul is chained, but the word is not.

insights.title: The next chapter
insights.body: Acts has no proper ending; the witness continues. What part of that story is yours to carry on?

intro.who: It is the second volume by the author of Luke, again addressed to Theophilus (1:1). Passages told as "we" suggest he travelled with Paul, and tradition names Luke; most scholars accept one author for both books, while debating whether he was Paul's companion.
intro.when: The story runs from Jesus' ascension, about AD 30, to Paul under guard in Rome around AD 62. Some date the writing to the early 60s, since it ends there; many prefer about AD 80–90.
intro.why: It shows the risen Jesus continuing his work through the Spirit, as witness spreads from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth (1:8), and that welcoming Gentiles was God's plan all along.
